findings.paper_title: Schools' Forum DFC Balances Update Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: 11 schools exceeded three-year Devolved Formula Capital holding limit by £110,926 as at 31 August 2026, risking DfE clawback
findings.detail: Eleven schools had exceeded the three-year limit for holding Devolved Formula Capital as at 31 August 2026, with overly-aged balances totalling £110,926. The council has advised these schools of the risk that the DfE may claw back excess balances. Overall, the council's combined balance was within the allowable total, so no immediate clawback is applicable.
findings.matters: Unspent capital funding may be reclaimed by the funder; managing capital spending to avoid clawback is a resource governance duty
findings.figures: 11 schools, £110,926 in overly-aged balances, three-year allowance threshold

findings.paper_title: Schools' Forum DFC Balances Update Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Excess school surplus balances decreased by £786,000 to £8.8 million; 20 schools exceed permitted thresholds, down from 24 in prior year
findings.detail: The council actively manages schools' excess surpluses through written inquiry. The total excess surplus fell from £9.6 million (24 schools) in 2024-2025 to £8.8 million (20 schools) in 2025-2026. All 20 schools holding excess surpluses submitted responses to the council's 11 September 2026 deadline. Current financial information indicates school balances will reduce further in 2026-2027.
findings.matters: Excess surpluses represent unused capacity or inefficient resource deployment; active management of these is a governance indicator
findings.figures: £8.8 million total (down from £9.6 million); 20 schools exceeding thresholds (down from 24); changes by type: Nurseries +£43,000, Primary -£287,000, Secondary -£1.03 million, Special +£491,000
findings.quote: The total excess surplus balances have decreased overall by £786,000 from a total of £9.6 million reported in 2024-2025 to £8.8million in 2025-2026.

findings.paper_title: Schools' Forum DFC Balances Update Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Two schools entered deficit for first time in 2025-2026; eight schools in deficit with external support programme temporarily suspended
findings.detail: Eight schools reported deficits in 2025-2026, including two entering deficit for the first time and four in ongoing recovery from prior-year deficits. Four schools in recovery received support from the DfE's Schools Resource Management Advisory Programme (SRMA) in summer 2026; however, the DfE has temporarily suspended the SRMA programme while considering a new approach. The council will provide direct support to the two newly-identified deficit schools.
findings.matters: School deficits consume council resources; suspension of external support adds pressure on the council's capacity to manage recovery
findings.figures: 8 schools in deficit at 31 March 2026: 2 new entries, 4 in ongoing recovery, 2 in existing monitoring recovery; SRMA advisor visits in summer 2026, programme now temporarily suspended
findings.quote: Of the eight schools reporting a deficit in 2025-2026, two schools are in a deficit position for the first time.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1
findings.headline: In-City independent SEND provision for Pre-16 pupils increased 17% while out-of-city provision fell 7%

findings.matters: A shift toward in-city placements indicates either changing pupil needs or market dynamics in independent provision. In-city provision is typically more costly than out-of-city, so a shift signals rising placement costs and a changing budget dynamic.

findings.headline: St Matthias School carries a deficit balance of £15,489.58 as at 31 August 2026
findings.detail: The secondary school spent £42,538.50 in the first five months of the year, exceeding its opening balance of £27,048.92 and allocation of £18,208.75 combined. findings.matters: A school operating with a deficit balance raises questions about spending control and financial sustainability; the council must determine how the shortfall will be recovered and whether there are underlying management issues requiring intervention.

findings.paper_title: DSG Outturn 2025-2026
findings.headline: Schools Block surplus of £0.5 million driven by growth fund timing slippage and non-implementation of planned bulge classes
findings.detail: The Schools Block achieved an in-year surplus of £0.5 million, primarily from underspend in the growth fund. This was caused by delays in receipt of validated Spring Census data and by anticipated bulge class implementations not materializing as planned. The surplus does not reflect structural efficiency but rather timing of one-off capital expansion commitments.
findings.matters: While positive, the surplus masks timing of school place planning commitments rather than delivering recurring savings, so it is unlikely to offset the structural High Needs deficit in future years.
findings.figures: £0.5 million in-year Schools Block surplus; £1.6 million growth fund expenditure in year against £(1.6) million implied allocation
findings.quote: The in-year surplus is as a result of an underspend in the growth fund in the financial year 2025-2026 which was reported in the growth fund update report presented at Schools' Forum in January. The underspend was as a result of the timing of the receipt of validated Spring Census data and due to some of the bulge classes not being implemented as anticipated.

findings.paper_title: DSG Outturn 2025-2026
findings.headline: Top-up funding, exceptional needs, and alternative provision costs accelerating, pointing to rising demand for specialist education places
findings.detail: Within the High Needs overspend, top-up funding for pupils in mainstream settings rose £2.7 million (10%) year-on-year. Exceptional needs funding, supporting bespoke one-to-one support and specialist equipment, increased £340,000 (15%). Alternative provision overspent its budget by £330,000 (43%), including £310,000 of additional funding for Speech and Language services directly commissioned. In special schools and alternative provisions combined, additional expenditure reached £1.9 million.
findings.matters: Multiple cost lines within High Needs rising simultaneously—top-up, exceptional needs, and alternative provision—suggest structural demand growth for specialist places rather than one-off pressures, a concern replicated across many councils facing similar SEND inflation.
findings.figures: £2.7 million (10%) top-up increase; £340,000 (15%) exceptional needs increase; £330,000 (43%) alternative provision overspend; £1.9 million special schools/AP additional spend; £578,000 primary/secondary additional spend; £115,000 post-16 additional spend
findings.quote: The expenditure against Top-up funding increased by £2.7 million (10%). This increase in expenditure was part of the overspend indicated for quarter three. In primary and secondary settings overall, there was an additional spend of £578,000, in special schools and alternative provisions settings there was an additional spend of £1.9 million and post 16 saw an additional spend of £115,000.

findings.paper_title: DSG Outturn 2025-2026
findings.headline: DSG unusable reserve deficit grew to £9.2 million at year-end, a £4.3 million deterioration from prior year, with High Needs overspend overwhelming Schools and Early Years surpluses
findings.detail: Schools Block delivered a £0.5 million in-year surplus and Early Years Block a £0.4 million underspend. However, the High Needs Block's £10.4 million deficit exceeded these surpluses, resulting in a net DSG deficit of £9.2 million recorded in the unusable reserve. The cumulative deficit position worsened from £4.9 million at the end of 2024-2025, an adverse movement of £4.3 million in a single year.
findings.matters: An accumulating DSG deficit that is growing year-on-year indicates unsustainable spending in High Needs provision that will eventually require council general fund support or service reductions, a sustainability issue closely watched by finance counterparts and lenders.

findings.matters: A High Needs deficit that expanded unexpectedly mid-year signals structural demand pressure in SEN provision that will require either increased DSG funding or further reductions in service, a pressure affecting many councils.

findings.paper_title: 06. Appendix 1 WMPF Audit Findings Report 25-26 Draft
findings.headline: £14.1m of early retirement costs relating to 2024/25 were recorded in 2025/26, identified by auditors as breach of Fund's accounting policy
findings.detail: Audit testing of contributions receivable identified that £14.1m of early retirement costs should have been recognised in 2024/25 (when liability arose) but were instead recorded in 2025/26, contrary to the Fund's stated accounting policy. Management assessment concluded the amount is immaterial, no prior year restatement was made. Auditors raised a recommendation that management ensure transactions are recognised in line with accounting policies.
findings.matters: Cut-off errors in contributions receivable affect income recognition and can distort year-on-year comparisons of contribution funding between periods.
findings.figures: £14.1m early retirement costs; 2024/25 liability recorded in 2025/26
findings.quote: As part of our testing of employer contributions receivable, we identified that £14.1m of early retirement costs relating to 2024/25 were recorded in 2025/26. The Fund's accounting policy states that employer's augmentation contributions and pensions strain contributions are accounted for in the period in which the liability arises.

findings.paper_title: 06. Appendix 1 WMPF Audit Findings Report 25-26 Draft
findings.headline: Auditors identified £20.7m unadjusted difference in Level 3 investment valuations, assessed as immaterial by management despite exceeding reporting threshold
findings.detail: Audit testing identified a £20.7m overstatement in valuation of Level 3 investments (financial assets) due to timing of information availability for pension fund reporting compared to the underlying investment fund audit date. Management concluded the difference is not material both quantitatively and qualitatively and did not adjust financial statements. The identified amount exceeds the £10.9m reporting threshold.
findings.matters: Investment valuations represent the majority of pension fund assets, and identified discrepancies between reported and auditor-assessed values indicate potential measurement or process weaknesses.
findings.figures: £20.7m unadjusted difference in investments; £10.9m reporting threshold
findings.quote: We however identified £20.7m of unadjusted differences in the valuation of the Fund's investments disclosed in the financial statements and/or Fund Account as at 31 March 2026. Management are proposing not to amend the financial statements on the basis that the differences are not material both quantitatively and qualitatively.

findings.paper_title: 06. Appendix 1 WMPF Audit Findings Report 25-26 Draft
findings.headline: West Midlands Pension Fund self-reported missing 31 August 2025 deadline for Annual Benefit Statements; 80% active, 93% deferred produced by August 2026
findings.detail: The Fund was required to issue Annual Benefit Statements to active, deferred, and pension credit members within 5 months of scheme year-end. West Midlands Pension Fund took the decision to self-report this breach. As at August 2026, the Fund had produced statements for 80% of active members and 93% of deferred members, with management reviewing reasons for non-production.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance on member communications is fundamental to pension fund governance and is directly monitored by the Pensions Regulator.
findings.figures: 31 August 2025 (statutory deadline); 80% active members, 93% deferred members produced by August 2026
findings.quote: the Pension Fund took the decision to self-report to the Pensions Regulator for the production of Annual Benefit Statements for 2025. Under Regulation 89 (1) and (2) an administering authority must issue an Annual Benefit Statement to each of its active, deferred, deferred pension and pension credit members no later than 5 months after the end of the scheme year to which it relates (31st August). Unfortunately, West Midlands Pension Fund was unable to issue benefit statements to all of its active members by 31st August 2025.

findings.paper_title: 10. Appendix 1 Performance and Workload Dashboard
findings.headline: SCAPE factor change is halting pension casework and expected to worsen performance in coming months.
findings.detail: Retirement finalisation cases are currently on hold due to a SCAPE (Superannuation Contributions Adjusted for Past Experience) factor change. The fund explicitly flags this as 'expected to impact performance in the coming months.' SCAPE changes directly drive pension valuations and employer contribution rates. The paper does not quantify the scale of the performance impact or the contribution rate effect.
findings.matters: As an employer in the scheme, Wolverhampton's contributions are set by SCAPE and fund valuations. A change that degrades casework performance may indicate a broader revaluation cycle affecting the council's employer contribution liability and future budget.

findings.paper_title: 12. Quarterly Investment Report Final
findings.headline: WMTL scheme transitioning to 0% equities and 55% liability-driven investment by July 2027, from 17% equities and 26% LDI
findings.detail: The West Midlands Travel Limited (WMTL) admitted body scheme is transitioning from a balanced allocation (17% listed equities, 21% multi-asset credit, 26% LDI) to a purely defensive strategy (0% equities, 0% multi-asset credit, 55% LDI) effective 1 July 2027. This eliminates all growth assets in favour of liabilities hedging. The transition is described as driven by the pace of Private Debt commitment drawdowns, but the completed allocation represents a fundamental shift in investment posture.
findings.matters: Moving to zero equity exposure and maximum liability hedging may indicate either a scheme surplus being locked in or a deficit requiring conservative positioning, either way signalling a material change in the sponsor's or administrator's risk assessment of this former Wolverhampton-related scheme.
findings.figures: WMTL listed equities moving from 17% current to 0% by July 2027; LDI rising from 26% to 55%; multi-asset credit falling from 21% to 0%; private debt holdings (£49m) increasing as growth assets are withdrawn
findings.quote: WMTL is in the process of transitioning its allocation towards its final target allocation as commitments to Private Debt are drawn down. Interim targets have been put in place predicated on the expected pace of drawdown.

findings.paper_title: 12. Quarterly Investment Report Final
findings.headline: Infrastructure assets have experienced write-downs on legacy transport investments due to refinancing challenges
findings.detail: The Infrastructure portfolio has incurred actual impairments on historical transport sector assets facing refinancing difficulties. The portfolio generated 6.4% returns over one year but has been materially impacted by these write-downs over longer periods, contributing to underperformance of 1.9% per annum against its benchmark over 5 years.
findings.matters: Write-downs represent actual losses on fund investments and signal either poor past investment decision-making or deteriorating conditions in the transport infrastructure sector, both of which raise questions about fund governance and asset quality that lenders use to assess council financial stewardship.
findings.figures: Infrastructure portfolio 6.4% over 1 year but underperformed by 1.9% per annum over 5 years due to write-downs
findings.quote: Long-term performance has been subdued by write-downs on legacy transport assets linked to refinancing challenges, as well as the concentrated nature of the portfolio in its early years.

findings.paper_title: 12. Quarterly Investment Report Final
findings.headline: Active investment managers have underperformed their benchmarks consistently, with the Main Fund returning 13.0% over 12 months but trailing its benchmark by 2.4%
findings.detail: Sustained underperformance spans multiple asset classes and time periods. The LGPS Central Global Active Equity Fund underperformed by 3.2% per annum over 5 years; the Private Equity portfolio returned -3.2% in Q2 and has underperformed the FTSE All World Index by 2.9% per annum over 10 years. Even over the full 10-year period, the Main Fund trails its benchmark by 0.4% per annum. Passive equity funds have performed satisfactorily against their benchmarks, indicating the issue is with active manager selection, not market timing.
findings.matters: Persistent underperformance against actuarial assumptions and benchmarks will require higher employer contribution rates from Wolverhampton and other participant councils to meet funding targets, directly increasing pressure on council budgets.
findings.figures: 13.0% 12-month return, underperforming benchmark by 2.4%; LGPS Central Global Active Equity Fund down 3.2% per annum over 5 years; Private Equity -3.2% in Q2; Main Fund trails benchmark by 0.4% per annum over 10 years
findings.quote: Over the twelve months to quarter end, the Fund returned 13.0%, underperforming the benchmark by 2.4%. This shortfall was largely attributable to weaker relative performance from Listed Equities and Private Equity portfolios.

findings.paper_title: 08. Budget Monitoring and Quarterly Accounts to 30 June 2026 Final
findings.headline: Pension Fund net assets grew by £1.2 billion in Q1, driven by investment performance, indicating strong fund health and financial management.
findings.detail: Net assets increased from £23.4 billion at 31 March 2026 to £24.6 billion at 30 June 2026. The prior year saw investment returns of £2.263 billion. Investment management costs remain low at 0.41% of closing asset values, down from 0.48% in the prior year and below peer median performance.
findings.matters: Strong fund performance and growth demonstrate that pension liabilities are being met through investment returns and that the administering authority faces no unfunded pension obligations.
findings.figures: Assets £24.6bn (30 June 2026) vs £23.4bn (31 March 2026); investment return 2025/26 £2.263bn; investment fees 0.41% of assets (down from 0.48%)

findings.paper_title: 07. Appendix 1 WMPF Audit Findings Report 25-26
findings.headline: £14.1m early retirement costs recorded in wrong financial year
findings.detail: Early retirement costs of £14.1m relating to 2024/25 were recorded in 2025/26, contrary to the Fund's accounting policy requiring recognition in the period the liability arises. Correspondence from May 2025 shows the amount was known (estimated at £13m) before the prior year accounts were finalised, suggesting the accrual should have been made then. findings.matters: Year-end timing issues for material liabilities affect period comparability and suggest deficient finance controls; such cut-off errors can accumulate across multiple transactions.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Treasury Management Annual Report 2526 Activity Monitoring Quarter One 2627
findings.headline: Three LOBO loans totaling £17m were called in 2025-2026; the council repaid them at par rather than accept new rates of 6.19-6.26%
findings.detail: A £7m Commerzbank LOBO was called on 31 July 2025 with a new rate proposed of 6.19% versus the existing 3.60%. Two £5m Dexia LOBOs were called on 26 and 30 January 2026 with proposed rates of 6.21% and 6.26% versus existing rates of 4.26% and 4.29%. The council rejected all three proposals and repaid the loans. These calls represent a refinancing and liquidity event, requiring the council to secure £17m in cash to repay at par.
findings.matters: LOBO calls materialize the refinancing risk embedded in the council's debt portfolio. The high rates offered (60-173 basis points above existing rates) show market stress on LOBO lending at the time. A lender cares whether the council can refinance when forced to do so; the fact that the council had the liquidity to repay £17m at par demonstrates this capacity, but it also shows the council is exposed to repricing risk when the lender chooses to exercise options.

findings.headline: Majority of £8.4 million of approved savings targets on track for delivery in 2026-2027.
findings.detail: The council's 2026-2027 budget incorporates £8.4 million of approved savings targets, including minimum productivity and efficiency targets and one-off resources. Early indications show services are making good progress with the majority of savings on track for delivery.
findings.matters: Savings delivery demonstrates financial discipline and the council's ability to manage structural budget pressures; early-year tracking indicates whether the council is on trajectory.
findings.figures: £8.4 million approved savings targets
findings.quote: With regards to approved savings targets, early indications are that services are making good progress, with the majority of savings targets on track for delivery in this financial year.

findings.paper_title: 2026-2027 Q1 Presentation Scrutiny Board
findings.headline: Council set 2026-2027 balanced budget of £396.2 million without using general fund reserves, but faces emerging cost pressures in adult social care and resident services.
findings.detail: The council approved a balanced budget for 2026-2027 without drawing on general fund reserves, including £8.4 million of approved savings targets. However, early indications show emerging cost pressures, particularly in adult social care and resident services. Services identifying pressures are required to put in place recovery plans to mitigate them.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders assess financial sustainability partly by whether councils need to raid reserves to balance budgets; emerging cost pressures in social care are material given demographic demand and cost inflation.
findings.figures: £396.2 million net budget requirement; £8.4 million approved savings targets
findings.quote: The Council was again able to set a balanced budget for 2026-2027 without the need to use general fund reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Financial management risk score steady at 8/8; council depends on limited reserves to cushion expenditure overruns
findings.detail: The Financial Management risk notes that weak financial controls could cause expenditure to exceed budget, forcing a call on reserves. The council flags that its reserve position is limited. The risk score has not improved despite being on the register for years, suggesting this is a structural rather than cyclical concern.
findings.matters: Limited reserves and budget-overspend risk go together. A finance director needs to know how much reserve buffer the council has and whether it is being eroded by uncontrollable pressures.
findings.figures: Risk score 8/8 (current and target, unchanged); described as 'limited reserves'
findings.quote: If the Council does not have strong financial management there is a risk that the expenditure will exceed the budget, leading to a call on the limited reserves that are available to support the financial sustainability and transformation of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: CQC inspection outcome no longer poses risk of Inadequate rating; inspection completed June 2025, outcome awaited
findings.detail: The Care Quality Commission (CQC) conducted an onsite inspection of Adult Social Care in June 2025 and fed back positive informal comments with no serious concerns noted. The council received an updated (but not yet finalised) report in May 2026. As of the register update, the council is confident that an Inadequate rating is now very unlikely, and has downgraded the risk accordingly. Final outcome expected by 22 May 2026.
findings.matters: An Inadequate CQC rating would trigger enforcement and reputational damage. De-escalation of this risk is good news for financial and reputational resilience.
findings.figures: Risk score 6/6 (current and target, unchanged); onsite inspection June 2025; informal feedback no serious concerns
findings.quote: May 2026 – Updated report received but not yet finalised. Meeting held with CQC April 2026 with outcome expected by 22 May 2026. Inadequate rating now very unlikely, therefore risk scoring updated.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Agresso core financial system SaaS migration carries risk of implementation failure; system underpins all financial reporting and controls
findings.detail: The council's migration to Agresso as a Software-as-a-Service platform is at risk of slipping or implementation failure. The register notes this could significantly impact the council's core financial systems. Agresso holds all transactional financial data and sits at the heart of budget management, reporting, and audit controls. Risk score is 12/12.
findings.matters: A failed core financial system migration creates audit, compliance, and reporting risks. A finance director or auditor needs to know whether this is on track and whether there is a fallback plan.
findings.figures: Risk score 12/12 (current and target); no recent update on implementation progress visible
findings.quote: There is a risk the Council's Agresso SaaS migration is not successfully implemented in time resulting in the Council's core financial systems being significantly impacted and posing a reputational risk to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Energy from Waste plant holds highest risk score (20); no mitigation progress noted since March 2026
findings.detail: The council's Energy from Waste plant remains at maximum risk score (20/20). The risk is of non-operation due to major fire, breakdown, or unavailability of skilled contractors. This is a critical service and asset—failure would force waste diversion to alternative (expensive) disposal methods. Risk direction is unchanged (no improvement) and no update on mitigation progress is recorded in the June 2026 register.
findings.matters: A critical infrastructure asset at maximum risk with no visible improvement plan signals operational resilience exposure and potential cost shocks.
findings.figures: Risk score 20/20 (current and previous), target 9; risk rating unchanged since March 2026
findings.quote: There is a risk that the Energy from Waste (EfW) plant may become unavailable or non-operational, for example, due to significant fire or breakdown or the unavailability of a suitably skilled contractor to operate and maintain the plant.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Safeguarding Adults caseload increasing month-on-month; recruitment challenges in social work limiting response capacity
findings.detail: The Adult Social Care directorate is experiencing sustained month-on-month growth in safeguarding referrals. A restructure has now concluded but the transition phase is creating capacity pressures, compounded by difficulties recruiting suitably skilled social workers—agency staff are being used to fill gaps but supply is constrained. 45% of referrals are being assessed as inappropriate, but triaging them remains a workload.
findings.matters: A growing safeguarding caseload that cannot be staffed at pace creates a service delivery risk and a call on non-social-care budgets. It signals labour-market constraints beyond the council's control.
findings.figures: Month-on-month increase in referrals; 45% of referrals currently assessed as inappropriate; social workers and agency staff filling gaps; target risk score 6 (current and target)
findings.quote: There continues to be a month on month increase in Safeguarding referrals which impacts on the ability of Adult Social Care to ensure a timely response and has led to an increase in the time enquiries are taking. Whilst we have responded to the risks with additional temporary posts there are challenges with recruitment and shortage of suitably skilled agency social workers to fill temporary vacancies.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Private sector damp and mould complaints increased in winter 2024–25; service warns it cannot scale response without additional funding
findings.detail: Private rented housing damp and mould complaints have increased significantly again in the latest winter season after a high-demand winter 2023–24. The council's Private Sector Housing Service is responding reactively. The team explicitly warns that without additional resource and funding, serious mould cases cannot be treated as 'business as usual' and reactive management will continue. Cost-of-living pressures are deepening the problem.
findings.matters: Growing tenant health complaints in a sector the council has no direct control over but statutory duty for signals cost and resource risk. The explicit warning of inadequate funding is a flag.
findings.figures: Risk score 8/8 (current and target); serious complaint numbers increased winter 2024–25
findings.quote: Without additional resource and funding, dealing with serious mould cases cannot be established as a 'business as usual' work stream and the service will continue to respond reactively.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Social Housing Regulator issued C2 grading on 28 January 2026 citing weaknesses in consumer standards delivery; improvement required
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing graded the council C2 (Compliance with Concerns) with no serious failings noted, but in line with the council's own self-referral flagging weaknesses in delivering consumer standards outcomes. The council is now required to develop and deliver an Improvement Strategy with a Regulatory Compliance Board oversighting progress. The timing and pace of improvement delivery are under review.
findings.matters: A regulator-issued C rating creates enforcement risk and reputational exposure. It signals operational and governance weaknesses in a major asset base (council housing) and creates compliance costs.
findings.figures: C2 grading issued 28 January 2026; Impact score 4 (critical), likelihood score 4 (likely)
findings.quote: On 28 January 2026 the Regulator of Social Housing issued CWC a C2 grading, noting no serious failings, and in line with our self-referral that 'weaknesses in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards'

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Housing waiting list now exceeds 8,200 residents; council securing £19 million Homes England grant but supply-demand gap remains
findings.detail: Demand for council accommodation is increasing significantly with over 8,200 residents on the waiting list. The council faces pressure to place homeless households in temporary accommodation, a cost driver. However, the council has secured grant funding (first in the country for Homes England Portfolio Partner initiative providing up to £19 million) and is progressing multiple regeneration and new-build schemes. A 23% net increase in homes is targeted through estate masterplans.
findings.matters: A growing housing waiting list creates uncontrollable budget pressure through temporary accommodation spend. A lender needs to see whether the council has a credible plan to close the supply-demand gap and how long that will take.
findings.figures: Over 8,200 registered for council accommodation; £19 million Homes England Portfolio Partner grant; 23% net increase targeted through estate regeneration
findings.quote: the waiting list is increasing significantly (over 8200 registered for council accommodation), and vulnerable residents may need rehousing in temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Repairs budget overspend being driven by surge in damp and mould referrals; housing service faces resource constraints
findings.detail: Council-owned housing is experiencing a significant increase in damp and mould complaints, particularly in winter months. The council has had to reallocate staffing and financial resources to respond, but contractor capacity is constrained by regional labour shortages. The repairs budget is overspending as a result. The council notes 2% of inspections identify Category 1 hazards under HHSRS but cannot scale response without additional resources.
findings.matters: An emerging cost driver in an essential service signals both a budget risk and a latent capital/maintenance issue in the asset base. This affects reserves and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Risk score 8/8 (council properties), risk score 8/8 (private rented); 2% of DMC inspections classified as Category 1 hazard
findings.quote: Staffing and financial resources have needed to be reallocated to DMC to meet the increase in demand. Contractors have also been requested to increase labour resources. This has had limited success due to the region wide shortage in suitable labour. The repairs budget overspend is contributed to by DMC requests.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Medium-term financial planning risk reduced from 20 to 16, but three-year MTFS still faces demand and policy uncertainty to 2028–29
findings.detail: The council notes significant ongoing uncertainty around service demand, inflation, and impacts of proposed government policy changes over the next three financial years. The improved score from 20 to 16 suggests some mitigation, but the risk remains material. The council's MTFS planning is constrained by factors beyond its control including statutory service pressures and funding announcements.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to know whether a council can forecast and defend its budget over the medium term, and what external pressures threaten that stability.
findings.figures: Previous risk score 20 (March 2026), current score 16 (June 2026), target score 12; three-year planning horizon to 2028–29
findings.quote: There remains significant uncertainty in relation to demand for services, inflation and the impact of proposed changes to Government Policy, over the period of the MTFS, that being the next three years to 2028-2029.

findings.paper_title: Performance and Budget Monitoring Cabinet Covering Report
findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit of £14.1 million carried forward with statutory override extended to 2028 and High Needs Stability Grant pending.
findings.detail: The cumulative net Dedicated Schools Grant deficit to 31 March 2026 totalled £14.1 million, primarily reflecting Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) pressures in the High Needs Block. The statutory override allowing DSG deficits to be excluded from the council's wider financial position has been extended to 31 March 2028. The government announced a High Needs Stability Grant expected to cover up to 90% of the net deficit accrued as at 31 March 2026, but the amount remains unknown pending approval of a SEND reform plan.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is a systemic issue across councils; the timing and amount of the stability grant remains uncertain and creates medium-term financial risk.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit: £14.1 million; statutory override extended to: 31 March 2028; High Needs Stability Grant: up to 90% of accrued deficit
findings.quote: The cumulative net DSG deficit to 31 March 2026 totalled £14.1 million. The statutory override allowing DSG deficits to be excluded from the Council's wider financial position has been extended to 31 March 2028

findings.paper_title: Performance and Budget Monitoring Cabinet Covering Report
findings.headline: Pay award negotiations ongoing; budget risk if increase exceeds 3% assumption.
findings.detail: The 2026-2027 budget includes provision for a 3% pay award. In March 2026 national employers offered 3.3% for all grades. Chief Officers agreed to 3.3%, but at the time of the report, negotiations were still ongoing for all other pay grades. Any increase above the 3% budgeted would need to be funded from a combination of corporate contingencies, in-year efficiencies, and reserves, with recurrent impact built into future MTFS.
findings.matters: Pay cost overruns are a common source of budget pressure for councils; an unresolved negotiation at reporting date introduces near-term budget risk.
findings.figures: Budget assumption: 3%; offer made: 3.3%; Chief Officers approved: 3.3%; other grades: negotiations ongoing
findings.quote: At the time of writing, negotiations are still ongoing in respect of all other pay grades for 2026-2027 pay award. Any increase above the 3% currently built into the budgets for 2026-2026 would need to be funded from a combination of corporate contingencies, in year efficiencies and reserves

findings.paper_title: Performance and Budget Monitoring Cabinet Covering Report
findings.headline: External auditors report no significant weaknesses in Council's financial sustainability arrangements.
findings.detail: The council's external auditors (Grant Thornton) have confirmed they have not identified any significant weaknesses in the council's arrangements to ensure financial sustainability. The 2024-2025 audit received an unqualified audit opinion, with accounts presented fairly in all material respects. This positive validation supports the council's value for money arrangements.
findings.matters: Auditor validation of financial sustainability is a key assurance for lenders and external stakeholders; an unqualified opinion with no weaknesses identified is positive risk assessment.
findings.figures: 2024-2025 audit: unqualified opinion; 2025-2026 audit: pending
findings.quote: have not identified any significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements to ensure financial sustainability

findings.paper_title: Performance and Budget Monitoring Cabinet Covering Report
findings.headline: General Fund Balance maintained at £20 million cap; Enterprise Zone Business Rates Reserve drawn down by £5.5 million for Walsall Gasholder project.
findings.detail: The council's General Fund Balance is held at £20 million (either 5% of net budget or £20 million, whichever is lowest), having been increased by £954,000 in February 2026. Separately, approval is sought to draw £5.5 million from the Enterprise Zone Business Rates Reserve to fund the Walsall Gasholder scheme, with a further capped commitment of £14.5 million outstanding, subject to future business cases and surplus availability.
findings.matters: Reserve levels and their deployment indicate the council's confidence in its financial position and ability to manage shocks; drawing reserves for shared projects signals strategic decisions on capital allocation.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance: £20 million; Enterprise Zone reserve drawdown: £5.5 million; outstanding capped commitment: £14.5 million
findings.quote: On 25 February 2026, Full Council approved proposed change that the level which will be held in the General Fund Balance Reserve to either 5% of the net budget or £20.0 million, whichever is the lowest

findings.paper_title: Performance and Budget Monitoring Cabinet Covering Report
findings.headline: HRA forecast within budget for 2026-2027 with indication of lower borrowing costs than budgeted.
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is forecast to be within budget for 2026-2027. Early indications suggest the HRA may benefit from borrowing costs being lower than forecast. However, the council notes that the 30-year HRA business plan is unsustainable, and the council supports a national call for reform of the HRA framework, describing current pressures as a systemic issue rather than a failure of local delivery.
findings.matters: A council holding 21,000 homes faces structural borrowing pressures; while current year borrowing costs are improving, the flagged unsustainability of the 30-year plan signals ongoing strategic risk.
findings.figures: 21,000 council homes managed; HRA balance reserve: £16.3 million (13% of turnover, target minimum 10%)
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account (HRA) is forecast to be within budget for 2026-2027. Early indications suggest that the HRA may benefit from borrowing costs being lower than forecast

findings.paper_title: Performance and Budget Monitoring Cabinet Covering Report
findings.headline: Majority of 2026-2027 savings targets on track but some slippage and non-delivery identified.
findings.detail: The council approved £8.4 million of savings targets for 2026-2027 inclusive of £400,000 minimum productivity and efficiency targets. Early indications show the majority of these are on track for delivery, with some areas showing potential overachievement. However, a small number of savings targets are indicating potential slippage or non-delivery, which will be monitored and reported in future updates.
findings.matters: Savings delivery is critical to managing medium-term deficits; a council with mixed delivery on savings targets risks the medium-term position if slippage becomes widespread.
findings.figures: £8.4 million savings targets for 2026-2027; majority on track; some slippage identified
findings.quote: Early indications are that services are making good progress, with the majority of these savings targets on track for delivery in this financial year. A small number of these savings targets are indicating some potential slippage or non-delivery

findings.paper_title: Performance and Budget Monitoring Cabinet Covering Report
findings.headline: 2026-2027 tracking to balanced budget despite service pressures, with offsetting corporate budget efficiencies.
findings.detail: Early projections for 2026-2027 show emerging cost pressures mainly around increased demand and inflationary pressures in services including Adult Social Care, Children's in care, Public Health leisure, and Resident Services. However, overall the council is currently projecting a balanced budget as a result of efficiencies on corporate budgets, particularly Treasury Management. Contingency budgets held centrally totalling £3.3 million for savings delivery risks are currently assumed to be required in full.
findings.matters: A council tracking to balance despite emerging pressures shows effective management but leaves little room for further deterioration; the reliance on corporate budget efficiencies and contingencies being used in full indicates tightness.
findings.figures: Contingency for savings delivery risks: £3.3 million (assumed fully required); overall position: balanced
findings.quote: Despite pressures being identified in some services, overall as a result of efficiencies within some corporate budgets we are currently projecting a balanced budget for 2026-2027

findings.paper_title: Performance and Budget Monitoring Cabinet Covering Report
findings.headline: Emerging cost pressures in Adult Social Care from increased demand and rising care package costs.
findings.detail: Early forecasts indicate potential cost pressures within care purchasing budgets due to increased demand and cost of care packages. The council budgeted £12.5 million additional funding for Adult Social Care in 2026-2027 to cover inflationary and demand pressures. Services with emerging pressures are required to produce recovery plans to mitigate these budget pressures. A budget oversight board has been established to examine demand and cost pressures in detail.
findings.matters: Adult social care cost pressures are the most significant risk area for councils and are often difficult to control; this council is actively monitoring and has governance in place but pressures are emerging despite substantial investment.
findings.figures: £12.5 million additional budget approved for 2026-2027; pressures emerging despite this allocation
findings.quote: Early forecasts indicate some potential cost pressures within care purchasing budgets due to the increased demand and cost of care packages

findings.paper_title: Performance and Budget Monitoring Cabinet Covering Report
findings.headline: 2025-2026 revenue outturn was balanced after funding redundancy costs and reserve contributions.
findings.detail: The council achieved a balanced General Fund revenue outturn for the year ended 31 March 2026 after absorbing redundancy and pension strain costs and making contributions to both earmarked reserves and general balances. This was driven by additional one-off income, grants, and early delivery of Our Future Council savings.
findings.matters: Councils that consistently hit outturn targets demonstrate effective in-year budget management and are lower-risk borrowers; this result shows the council meeting its target despite spending pressures.
findings.figures: 2025-2026 General Fund outturn: balanced
findings.quote: General Fund revenue outturn position for 2025-2026 is a balanced budget after funding redundancy costs and making essential contributions to earmarked reserves and general balances

findings.paper_title: Performance and Budget Monitoring Cabinet Covering Report
findings.headline: Medium-term budget deficit forecast reduced from £23.5 million to £3.8 million in 2027-2028 through Our Future Council programme.
findings.detail: The council reported a projected deficit of £23.5 million in the previous year's budget. The current forecast for 2027-2028 is now £3.8 million, rising to £14.8 million in 2028-2029. This substantial improvement reflects early delivery of transformation savings through the Our Future Council programme, which has approved £31.8 million of recurrent savings over 2025-2026 to 2027-2028.
findings.matters: A finance director facing multi-year deficits would be closely watching whether improvement plans are delivering; this shows material progress but a significant gap remains to close.
findings.figures: £23.5 million → £3.8 million (2027-2028); £14.8 million (2028-2029); £31.8 million savings approved over three years
findings.quote: projected budget deficit of £3.8 million for 2027-2028 (compared to £23.5 million when modelled in the previous year's budget and MTFS report), rising to £14.8 million in 2028-2029

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 General Fund Budget Risks 20262027
findings.headline: Pay settlement negotiations for non-chief officer grades remain ongoing, creating uncertainty that contributes to 2026-27 Amber rating
findings.detail: While chief officer pay has been settled, negotiations for all other pay grades are still in progress. This outstanding pay settlement is cited as a factor in the overall 2026-27 budget risk being assessed as Amber.
findings.matters: Pay is typically the largest controllable cost element in a council budget; unresolved pay negotiations delay final budget certainty and create cost risk for the current financial year.
findings.figures: Chief officer pay award agreed; all other grades negotiations ongoing as of report date

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 General Fund Budget Risks 20262027

findings.matters: Policy-driven costs outside the council's control are a material risk to medium-term budget sustainability; a Red rating indicates the council expects these could significantly impact finances.
findings.figures: Government policy risks: Amber (2026-27), Red (MTFS period)
findings.quote: Risks that might materialise as a result of changes to Government policy, such as NHS restructuring, Social Care Fair Pay Policy, UK Emissions Trading Scheme, and the end of SEND statutory accounting override.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 General Fund Budget Risks 20262027
findings.headline: Statutory service demand risks, particularly adults' and children's social care and temporary accommodation, rated Red for medium term
findings.detail: The council identifies statutory service demand as a Red-rated risk for the MTFS period (Amber for 2026-27), specifically flagging concern that demand for social care and temporary accommodation could outstrip available resources.
findings.matters: Social care and temporary accommodation are historically the largest budget pressure areas for councils; a Red rating for these services in the medium term indicates material sustainability concerns.
findings.figures: Statutory service demands: Amber (2026-27), Red (MTFS period to 2028-2029)
findings.quote: Risks that might materialise as a result of demands for statutory services outstretching the available resources. This particularly applies to adults and children's social care, and temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 General Fund Budget Risks 20262027
findings.headline: Medium-term financial outlook (to 2028-2029) assessed as Red due to demand pressures, inflation costs and funding uncertainty
findings.detail: The council rates overall medium-term risks as Red, significantly higher than the Amber rating for 2026-2027. This Red assessment reflects concerns about increased demand, inflation costs and uncertainty around future funding that could materialise over the MTFS period.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender needs to understand the council's assessment of its medium-term financial sustainability; a Red rating signals material challenges the council expects to face beyond the current year.
findings.figures: MTFS period 2028-2029 assessed as Red; 2026-2027 assessed as Amber
findings.quote: the overall level of risks associated with Medium Term Financial Strategy up to 2028-2029 is currently assessed as Red mainly due to risks which might materialise as a result of increased demand, inflation costs and due to uncertainty around future funding

findings.quote: Early forecasts indicate some potential cost pressures within care purchasing budgets due to the increased demand and cost of care packages.

findings.detail: Serious complaints about damp and mould in private rentals increased year-on-year through winter 2024-25. findings.headline: Social housing regulator issued C2 rating with noted weaknesses requiring significant remediation
findings.detail: January 2026: Regulator of Social Housing gave the council a C2 grading (no serious failings but weaknesses noted). Regulator specifically flagged 'weaknesses in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards'. Multiple improvement tasks identified requiring 'significant focus'.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance failures in council housing can trigger enforcement action, financial penalties, and reputational damage. The council is managing a large housing stock (8,200+ on waiting list) under regulatory scrutiny.
findings.figures: C2 grading (January 28, 2026); risk score 8 (unchanged, target 8)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Capital projects face cost overrun, timing, and business-case alignment risks
findings.detail: The council acknowledges risks to ongoing capital projects (city centre regeneration, City Learning Quarter) in terms of costs, timings, and whether business cases continue to align with strategy. No quantified budget impacts given.
findings.matters: Capital project delivery risk directly affects council cash flow, borrowing needs, and return on investment. Lenders track whether councils deliver projects to budget.
findings.figures: Risk score 8 (unchanged, target 8)
findings.quote: There are risks to ongoing Council managed and operated capital projects and programmes in terms of costs, timings and ensuring that original business cases continue to align with the Council's strategic aims.

findings.headline: Agresso SaaS core financial system migration flagged as delivery risk; risk score 12 against target of 8
findings.detail: The Agresso SaaS migration is flagged as a delivery risk. If implementation slips, the council's core financial systems could be significantly impacted. Risk remains high at 12 with target of 8.
findings.matters: Core financial system stability is essential for managing council operations and financial reporting. A failed migration or missed deadline could disrupt financial controls and reporting.
findings.figures: Risk score 12 (target 8)
findings.quote: There is a risk the Council's Agresso SaaS migration is not successfully implemented in time resulting in the Council's core financial systems being significantly impacted and posing a reputational risk to the Council.

findings.headline: Equal pay claims pose unquantified contingent liability
findings.detail: The council faces potential exposure to equal pay claims arising from unapproved local working practices and new case law. No mitigation detail provided; risk score remains at maximum (12) with no improvement in sight.
findings.matters: Equal pay claims are open-ended contingent liabilities that can crystallize unpredictably and absorb significant council resources. Lenders need to understand scale and likelihood.
findings.figures: Risk score 12 (unchanged, target 12)
findings.quote: Due to potential unapproved local working practices, and new case law, there is a risk the Council could be exposed to future equal pay claims, thus impacting Council resources.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Medium-term financial strategy hinges on unknowns over next three years
findings.detail: The council is facing significant uncertainty about future demand for services, inflation, and government policy changes through 2028-2029. This uncertainty is stopping them from developing a robust financial plan. The risk score has improved from 20 to 16, but remains elevated at target 12.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the council can plan and manage finances reliably over the term of any loan. Admission of inability to develop a robust strategy is a material concern.
findings.figures: Risk score: 16 (down from 20, target 12); timeframe: three years to 2028-2029
findings.quote: There remains significant uncertainty in relation to demand for services, inflation and the impact of proposed changes to Government Policy, over the period of the MTFS, that being the next three years to 2028-2029. This uncertainty creates a risk that we cannot develop a robust medium term financial strategy.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) Risk Register
findings.headline: Pay negotiations ongoing for all pay grades except chief officers, creating budget uncertainty

findings.figures: Chief officers agreed; other grades negotiations ongoing

findings.headline: Business rates appeals pose specific income reduction risk rated Amber for both periods
findings.detail: The register specifically names successful appeals against business rates as a potential income loss. This is rated Amber for both 2026-2027 and MTFS period.
findings.matters: Business rates volatility directly affects the council's income base; successful appeals would force in-year budget rebalancing.
findings.figures: Amber for both 2026-2027 and MTFS period
findings.quote: The risk of successful appeals against business rates.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - 2026-2027 Budget and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) Risk Register
findings.headline: Savings delivery risk: non-delivery of approved savings targets rated Amber for both periods
findings.detail: The register identifies ongoing risk of delays or non-delivery of approved savings targets, rated Amber for both 2026-2027 and the MTFS period, indicating this is a sustained concern.
findings.matters: Budget delivery dependent on savings that may not materialise creates unplanned deficit risk if targets are missed.
findings.figures: Amber for 2026-2027; Amber for MTFS period
findings.quote: Risks that might materialise as a result of delays / non delivery of approved savings targets.

findings.headline: Statutory service demand pressures in social care and temporary accommodation rated Red for MTFS period
findings.detail: Demand risks for statutory services are rated Amber for 2026-2027 but Red for MTFS period. The register specifically names adults and children's social care and temporary accommodation as areas where demand might outstrip resources.
findings.matters: These are historically the largest budget risks in English councils; Red-rated demand for these services signals the council expects serious pressures in 2027-2029.
findings.quote: Risks that might materialise as a result of demands for statutory services outstretching the available resources. This particularly applies to adults and children's social care, and temporary accommodation.

findings.headline: MTFS period to 2028-2029 rated Red due to demand, inflation and funding uncertainty
findings.detail: The council's medium-term financial outlook faces a Red risk rating, with the register explicitly stating this is mainly due to increased demand, inflation costs and uncertainty around future funding. This contrasts with 2026-2027 which is Amber.
findings.matters: A Red MTFS rating indicates the council expects material budget viability risks to materialise in 2027-2029, which directly affects lending risk and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: MTFS 2028-2029 rated Red; 2026-2027 rated Amber
findings.quote: as reported to Cabinet in February 2026 the overall level of risks associated with Medium Term Financial Strategy up to 2028-2029 is currently assessed as Red mainly due to risks which might materialise as a result of increased demand, inflation costs and due to uncertainty around future funding.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - Treasury Management - Annual Report 2025-2026 and Activity Monitoring Quarter One 2026-2027
findings.headline: Service investment elements of prudential indicators forecast to exceed approved limits for 2027-2029.
findings.detail: The report flags that service investment components within the council's authorised limit and operational boundary are forecast to exceed the best estimates approved in February 2026. This is attributed to rephasing of capital programmes across years. While the overall limits remain within approved ceilings, the service investment component alone exceeds forecast. The council will review and re-set these limits at the next budget cycle.
findings.matters: Prudential indicators are self-imposed borrowing limits designed to ensure prudence. Exceeding forecasted components — even if within overall ceilings — suggests the council's capital planning visibility or control is tighter than current forecasts allow. A lender watches whether councils stay within their own self-determined limits, as drift signals loss of control.
findings.figures: Service investment elements forecast to slightly exceed best estimates for 2028-2029 (authorised limit) and 2027-2028 and 2028-2029 (operational boundary)
findings.quote: with regards 'PI 3 – Authorised limit for external debt' the forecast for 2028-2029 for service investments is slightly in excess of the best estimate presented to Council in the Treasury Management Strategy in February 2026. Likewise, 'PI 4 – Operational boundary for external debt' is in a similar position for service investments in 2027-2028 and 2028-2029.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - Treasury Management - Annual Report 2025-2026 and Activity Monitoring Quarter One 2026-2027
findings.headline: Three LOBO loans were called and rejected as lenders offered penalty rates; council managing debt in stressed market.
findings.detail: During 2025-2026, three Lender Option Borrower Option loans totalling £17 million were called. Lenders offered new rates ranging from 6.19% to 6.26%, significantly above the loans' current rates (3.60% to 4.29%). Wolverhampton rejected all proposals and repaid the loans instead. This shows the council is watchful for lender opportunism but also signals the debt refinancing market is becoming challenging.
findings.matters: LOBO calls with punitive rates are a stress signal in the public debt market. A lender to the council needs to understand that refinancing older borrowing is becoming more expensive and that the council is actively managing to avoid being trapped into higher rates. This affects future borrowing costs.
findings.figures: £17.0 million total LOBO principal called; proposed rates 6.19%, 6.21%, 6.26% versus current rates of 3.60%, 4.26%, 4.29%
findings.quote: Due to current market conditions some LOBO lenders are 'calling' their options and offering inflated long term rates deliberately set unattractively high so it would not be accepted. In order to be prudent, the potential for these 'calls' are included in the Council's cashflow projections to ensure that if called, the Council are in a position to repay the loans to avoid these higher rates.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - Treasury Management - Annual Report 2025-2026 and Activity Monitoring Quarter One 2026-2027
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased £42.3m to £1,152.2m; HRA borrowing up £63.5m, General Fund down £21.2m
findings.detail: The council's underlying need to borrow for capital purposes increased from £1,109.9 million to £1,152.2 million during 2025-2026. The split shifted: HRA (housing) borrowing need grew £63.5 million while General Fund fell £21.2 million. This means more of future borrowing will service housing rather than general services.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand what's driving borrowing growth. This shows the council's capital programme — particularly housing — is larger than originally forecast and will require proportionally more HRA revenue to service. HRA borrowing ratios and housing schemes carrying their own borrowing risk matter to credit analysis.
findings.figures: CFR increased £42.3 million (1,109.9 to 1,152.2); HRA CFR up £63.5 million; General Fund CFR down £21.2 million
findings.quote: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) increased from £1,109.9 million to £1,152.2 million throughout 2025-2026. This reflects a net increase in the Council's underlying need to borrow for capital purposes of £42.3 million. This was split between the General Fund and HRA at a rate of 56% and 44% respectively.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Managing Our Money Well - Treasury Management - Annual Report 2025-2026 and Activity Monitoring Quarter One 2026-2027
findings.headline: Council secured £20 million-plus long-term saving through debt rescheduling.
findings.detail: Wolverhampton repaid £55.8 million of fixed market debt held with Barclays at a discount during 2025-2026. The refinancing is projected to deliver savings in excess of £20 million over the next 40 years. This was a material opportunity captured during the year.
findings.matters: A lender tracking council financial health looks for evidence of prudent debt management and active refinancing to control long-term interest costs. This shows Wolverhampton is watching its debt portfolio and acting opportunistically.
findings.figures: £55.8 million repaid; projected savings over £20.0 million over the next 40 years
findings.quote: A debt rescheduling opportunity was undertaken during the year, repaying the fixed market debt of £55.8 million held with Barclays at a discount, which is projected to result in potential savings of over £20.0 million over the next 40 years.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme - Budget Outturn 2025-2026 including Quarter One Budget Monitoring 2026-2027
findings.headline: Capital programme rated as amber risk overall, with strategic MTFS risk from demand uncertainty and government funding volatility
findings.detail: The council's Strategic Risk Register continues to rate the overall capital programme risk as amber. The primary driver is uncertainty in the Medium Term Financial Strategy around demand for services, inflation, and levels of government funding—the same funding sources the capital programme depends on.
findings.matters: Amber risk rating on capital combined with acknowledged MTFS uncertainty signals management concern about both programme delivery and the funding environment; this constrains the council's financial resilience
findings.figures: £396m total borrowing planned; 66.1% of capital dependent on government grants
findings.quote: The overall risk associated with the programme continues to be quantified as amber.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme - Budget Outturn 2025-2026 including Quarter One Budget Monitoring 2026-2027
findings.headline: Two-thirds of capital funding is dependent on bid-reliant external grants with single-year settlements
findings.detail: 66.1% of the General Fund capital programme (£275.9m of £417.4m) is funded by external resources, predominantly single-year grants from central government and the West Midlands Combined Authority. The council notes this reliance and the bid-dependent nature contributes to programme profile uncertainty.
findings.matters: Heavy dependency on bid-reliant, single-year grant funding creates significant downside risk; if grant applications fail or funding is delayed, the council has limited internal resources to substitute and may have to cut capital delivery or increase borrowing
findings.figures: External resources 66.1% of General Fund capital financing; £269.5m of programme initially funded externally, increased to £275.9m in latest forecast
findings.quote: As the external resources, most significantly grants from central government and the WMCA, represent 66.1% of budget financing, the prevalence of single-year funding settlements and bid-reliant applications for funding also contributes to this profile.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme - Budget Outturn 2025-2026 including Quarter One Budget Monitoring 2026-2027
findings.headline: Capital delivery underperformed in 2025-2026, with 21% of General Fund budget re-profiled to future years
findings.detail: General Fund capital delivery reached only 79.1% of approved budget (£70.2m spent of £88.8m approved), with £18.6m re-profiled into later years in line with financial challenge priorities. This shows execution risk against the planned capital programme.
findings.matters: Persistent capital slippage affects the council's ability to deliver planned projects on time and can signal project management or resource constraints; re-profiling also defers income generation from capital assets
findings.figures: 2025-2026 General Fund: £70.2m outturn vs £88.8m approved = 79.1% delivery; £18.6m re-profiled
findings.quote: The outturn 2025-2026 expenditure for existing General Fund capital investment projects totals £70.2 million, representing delivery of the investment programme at 79.1% against the approved budget of £88.8 million.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme - Budget Outturn 2025-2026 including Quarter One Budget Monitoring 2026-2027
findings.headline: Asset maintenance contingency is insufficient for full replacement costs
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that the Corporate Provision and Contingency for Future Programmes budget is inadequate to fund the full extent of costs needed for maintaining and replacing council assets, even after asset rationalisation efforts.
findings.matters: Insufficient contingency to cover asset maintenance suggests a deteriorating asset base, future unfunded liabilities, and heightened risk of emergency capital calls or service-affecting deferrals
findings.figures: Total capital programme: £417.4m General Fund + £577.8m HRA
findings.quote: However, it should be noted that this resource is not sufficient to fund the full extent of the potential costs of maintaining and replacing our assets.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme - Budget Outturn 2025-2026 including Quarter One Budget Monitoring 2026-2027
findings.headline: Construction cost pressures are already realising and impacting capital project budgets
findings.detail: The council reports that rising construction costs in materials, labour and supply chain disruptions are actively impacting project budgets now, not just as a future risk. The council acknowledges significant uncertainty remains about future cost pressures and is monitoring their ongoing impact.
findings.matters: Materialising cost pressures on a £396m borrowing programme could lead to overspends, delivery delays, and reduced financial flexibility to manage the capital programme within budgeted borrowing
findings.figures: Increases in material costs already being realised; £102.8m General Fund borrowing plus £293.5m HRA borrowing planned through 2030-2031
findings.quote: There remains significant uncertainty and cost pressures which continue to affect the capital investment programme. Rising construction costs – particularly in materials, labour and supply chain disruptions – are already impacting project budgets.

findings.paper_title: Our Future Council: Investing in Our City - Capital Investment Programme - Budget Outturn 2025-2026 including Quarter One Budget Monitoring 2026-2027
findings.headline: Council is under financial stress and restructuring capital delivery to find revenue savings
findings.detail: Wolverhampton established its 'Our Future Council' programme in November 2024 explicitly 'in recognition of the extent of the financial challenge the Council faces'. The capital programme is being reviewed to identify opportunities to generate revenue budget savings (noted twice in the recommendations). Asset rationalisation is being used to reduce costs and generate capital receipts.
findings.matters: A council restructuring its capital and revenue delivery due to financial challenges signals constrained financial position and raises questions about the ability to service increased debt
findings.figures: £396m total prudential borrowing planned (£102.8m General Fund + £293.5m HRA through 2030-2031)
findings.quote: In November 2024, Cabinet approved the approach and guiding principles of Our Future Council (OFC) in recognition of the extent of the financial challenge the Council faces.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Assessment of Going Concern
findings.headline: Capital investment programme experiencing cost inflation and supply chain pressure
findings.detail: The council's multi-year capital programme (£352.6 million across 2024-25 to 2029-30) faces material cost pressures from construction market conditions. Rising costs in materials, labour, and supply chain disruptions are impacting project budgets. The council monitors but has not published mitigation.
findings.matters: Multi-year capital commitments can significantly impact future revenue if projects overrun or require accelerated borrowing. Sustained cost inflation in the construction sector could force repricing or deferral of planned investment.
findings.figures: Medium-term capital programme £352.6 million (2024-25 to 2029-30); 2025-2026 outturn £70.2 million against revised budget £87.1 million
findings.quote: There remains significant uncertainty and cost pressures which continue to affect the capital investment programme. Rising construction costs, particularly in materials, labour and supply chain disruptions are impacting on project budgets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Assessment of Going Concern
findings.headline: Children's social care cost growth is explicitly flagged as a particular challenge
findings.detail: Among medium-term pressures facing the council (including pay inflation and general demand growth), increases in children's social care costs are specifically identified as a particular challenge. The council also faces increased demand pressures in adult social care.
findings.matters: Children's social care is demand-driven, difficult to control, and a known area of overspend across councils. Its specific callout here suggests the council views it as a material risk that may continue to drive budget pressures despite savings plans.
findings.figures: 2026-2027 budget £396.2 million; savings targets £8.4 million
findings.quote: Like many other local authorities, the Council continues to be faced with pressures over the medium term, such as pay and other inflationary related pressures, increases in costs within children's social care being a particular challenge.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Assessment of Going Concern
findings.headline: Medium-term deficit projections improved significantly after funding settlement, but deficits remain forecast for 2027-2028 and 2028-2029
findings.detail: In February 2025, the council projected a £23.5 million deficit for 2027-2028. Following the February 2026 funding settlement (Fair Funding Review), this projection improved to £3.8 million for the same year, though it then rises to £14.8 million by 2028-2029. This material improvement in outlook reflects changes to central government funding allocation favouring higher-deprivation councils.
findings.matters: Lenders assess councils' medium-term sustainability through multi-year projections. The improvement is positive but the remaining deficits show continued financial challenges that must be managed through delivery of the council's Our Future Council savings programme.
findings.figures: 2027-2028 deficit: £23.5 million (Feb 2025 projection) reduced to £3.8 million (Feb 2026 projection); 2028-2029 projected deficit £14.8 million
findings.quote: In February 2026, it was reported that the updated projected budget deficit was £3.8 million for 2027-2028 (compared to £23.5 million previously), rising to £14.8 million by 2028-2029.

findings.paper_title: Final Audit and Risk Committee Report - Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026
findings.headline: All 17 Financial Management Code standards now assessed as green after improvement of one previously amber standard
findings.detail: The Council conducted a self-assessment against CIPFA's 17 Financial Management Code standards. One standard that was previously assessed as amber (requiring improvement) has been reviewed and updated. That standard has now moved to green, meaning all 17 standards are now assessed as green, demonstrating full compliance.
findings.matters: The Financial Management Code is a formal framework designed to identify risks to financial sustainability and demonstrates the council's compliance with standards for good financial management practice.
findings.figures: All 17 standards now green (previously 16 green, 1 amber)
findings.quote: This standard have been reviewed and updated, which have resulted in the final standard moving from amber to green. This has resulted in all 17 standards now assessed as green.

findings.headline: Future Years Budget Strategy Reserve held with £2m already committed for forward spending
findings.detail: The council holds £7.6m in this reserve specifically to 'support the budget strategy in future years,' with £2m already approved for commitment. This indicates the council expects budget pressures ahead and is building a specific buffer to manage them.

findings.detail: Schools balances fell from £13.4m to £11.7m with a transfer out of £4.4m. This represents significant drawdown from what may be a key buffer against rising school spending pressures, particularly given national cost pressures in education.

findings.detail: Sustainable MTFS Reserve increased by £2.6m (7.1m to 9.8m) and Our City Our Plan Reserve increased by £5.1m (3.0m to 8.2m). These reserves fund the 'Our Future Council Transformation Strategy' to 'deliver greater efficiencies.' The scale of addition suggests significant planned restructuring or confidence in future savings.
